newsitem.title: UK: UK publishes draft law on share buy-back tax.
newsitem.headline: UK publishes draft law on share buy-back tax.

text.p: Britain's taxation authority, the Inland Revenue, on Thursday published the draft legislation, which will be included in the next Finance Bill, on companies buying their own shares or paying special dividends.
The legislation will carry out the announcement made by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Kenneth Clarke, in October.
Clarke's proposal will change the treatment of particular transactions so there will be no payable tax credit.
The income tax liability of taxpayers who receive distributions will be largely unaffected by the change.
However, shareholders, such as pension funds, who were previously eligible for payments of tax credits, will no longer be able to claim them, the Revenue said in a statement.

The draft legislation deals with the treatment of distributions when a company purchases its own shares, or where a distribution is linked to a transaction in securities. Where such distributions are made, they will be treated in the same way as foreign income dividends.
It said certain types of dividend would not normally fall within the new rules.
These are, broadly, the payment of cash as an alternative to a stock dividend, dividends on fixed-rate preference shares and ordinary pre-sale dividends.
In addition, group income elections can be made in respect of dividends which are within the new legislation, providing the company paying the dividend is a wholly-owned subsidiary.
Generally, where a company pays a premium to purchase its own shares, this is seen as a distribution of profits, as is any special dividend payment.
As a result the company has to account for advance corporation tax and a tax credit is made available, by the Exchequer, to the recipient of the distribution.
The tax credit is sufficient to cover any liability to lower or basic-rate tax. Higher-rate taxpayers have additional tax to pay while those who are exempt can obtain a tax credit.
Under the proposed changes, the position of taxpayers will remain largely unaffected.
They will receive distributions which are treated as having borne lower-rate income tax. That income tax will not, however, be repayable, and there will be no payable tax credit.
Clarke's announcement in October caused Reuters Holdings Plc to postpone indefinitely a plan to return 613 million stg to shareholders via a share buy-back and special bonus dividend.
